subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Copernicus: The Sun at the Center
description: Learn Copernicus: The Sun at the Center in one minute.

hook.text: In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus published a book that removed Earth from the center of the universe.

buildup.text: His model placed the Sun at the center, with Earth and the other planets orbiting around it.

discovery.text: The heliocentric model simplified planetary motion. Retrograde loops that baffled Ptolemy became simple geometry.

twist.text: Copernicus delayed publication until he was dying. His book arrived on his deathbed—he may never have read it.

climax.text: The Catholic Church later banned his book. It stayed on the forbidden list for over 200 years.

punchline.text: Published on his deathbed. Banned for two centuries. Correct all along.

quiz.question: What did Copernicus propose in his 1543 book?
options: That the Sun, not Earth, was at the center of the planetary system
That the universe is infinite with no center
That planets orbit in perfect circles around Earth

details.summary: Nicolaus Copernicus published 'De Revolutionibus' in 1543, proposing that the Sun — not Earth — sits at the center of the solar system, with planets orbiting around it.
details.whyItMatters: The Copernican Revolution displaced Earth and humanity from the cosmic center, fundamentally changing our understanding of our place in the universe.
takeaways: Copernicus proposed the Sun, not Earth, is the center
His 1543 book launched the Scientific Revolution
He still used circular orbits, not yet achieving full accuracy

faq.question: Why did Copernicus wait so long to publish?
faq.answer: He feared ridicule from fellow scholars and potential religious backlash. His book was published near his death in 1543 — legend says he received the first printed copy on his deathbed.

faq.question: Was Copernicus's model actually more accurate than Ptolemy's?
faq.answer: Initially, not much. Both used circular orbits and epicycles, so predictions were similar. The heliocentric model's advantage was conceptual simplicity — it naturally explained retrograde motion and planetary brightness variations. True accuracy came later with Kepler's elliptical orbits.
